value.overview: The Orinoco Goose is a large, distinctive sheldgoose of tropical South America. It is strongly associated with rivers, oxbow lakes, marshes, sandy banks, and nearby savanna or open woodland. Unlike many geese, it spends much time walking and grazing on land and often perches in trees. The species is usually seen in pairs or small family groups and is generally quiet and wary. In Costa Rica, it is an exceptionally rare accidental visitor rather than a regular native species.
value.classification: The Orinoco Goose belongs to the duck and goose family Anatidae and the order Anseriformes. It is often placed in the genus Oressochen, although some taxonomic authorities use Neochen jubata. It is considered monotypic, with no widely recognized subspecies.
value.identification: This is a medium-large goose, about 56–66 cm long, with a heavy body, long legs, and a relatively short bill. Adults have a dark head and upperparts, a contrasting pale or whitish throat and lower face, rich chestnut-brown coloration across the breast and flanks, and darker wings and tail. The sexes look alike, although females are slightly smaller. It usually walks upright on riverbanks and grasslands and may sit in trees. Costa Rican records require careful documentation because confusion with escaped waterfowl is possible.
value.rangeHabitat: The normal range extends across tropical South America east of the Andes, including parts of Venezuela, Colombia, Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, Paraguay, and northern Argentina. It uses broad rivers, river islands, sandy beaches, marshes, forest lakes, oxbows, gallery forest, savanna, and open woodland, generally in lowland or foothill settings. Costa Rica lies outside its established native range. The species is listed there as rare or accidental, so records represent exceptional vagrancy or possible escape or release, not a resident population.
value.migrationStatus: Mostly resident, but some populations make local or regional seasonal movements, especially after breeding or in response to changing water levels. There is no reliable evidence that Costa Rica forms part of a regular migration route; occurrences there are accidental and highly unusual.
value.breeding: Orinoco Geese usually breed as territorial pairs during a season influenced by rainfall and local hydrology. They commonly nest in cavities in large trees, including hollow trunks or branches, but may occasionally nest on the ground. The female generally lays about 7–10 eggs, and incubation lasts roughly four weeks. Adults remain protective around the nest and lead their precocial young to nearby water and feeding areas. No established breeding population is known from Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: The species is primarily herbivorous. It grazes on grasses, sedges, leaves, shoots, seeds, and other tender vegetation in open areas beside water. It may also take aquatic plants and algae, particularly around stagnant water, oxbows, and river margins. Feeding is mainly terrestrial and often occurs during the day, with movements between resting and feeding sites around dawn and dusk. Small invertebrates may be taken occasionally, but they are not the main food.
value.behavior: Orinoco Geese are generally terrestrial, walking and grazing more often than swimming. They frequently occur in pairs or small family groups and may rest or roost in trees, on exposed riverbanks, or on sandy islands. Breeding pairs defend territories and can become aggressive toward intruders. The birds are wary and usually fly only when disturbed or traveling between sites. Some populations make seasonal movements along river systems, and individuals may travel at night during these movements.

conservation.populationTrend: The global trend is not fully resolved. Declines have been reported in parts of the range, while some populations, particularly in Brazil, appear stable or increasing; the overall population is therefore best described as locally declining or uncertain rather than clearly stable.
conservation.threats: Important pressures include conversion and degradation of river margins, sandy breeding and roosting beaches, wetlands, gallery forest, and adjacent grasslands. Hunting and local collection for meat can affect some populations, while disturbance near nesting areas and disruption of seasonal movements may also reduce breeding success. Because Costa Rica supports no known established population, local conservation concerns there mainly involve accurate documentation and preventing the release of captive or non-native waterfowl.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect rivers, wetlands, oxbow lakes, sandy banks, gallery forest, and nearby natural grasslands across the species’ South American range. Support protected areas and management that limits hunting and disturbance at nesting and roosting sites. In Costa Rica, report any suspected Orinoco Goose to a recognized bird-records committee or conservation organization with photographs, location, date, and notes on origin; do not release captive waterfowl into the wild.
